L7: Function calling (also known as tool calling) provides a powerful and flexible way for OpenAI models to interface with external systems and access data outside their training data. This guide shows how you can connect a model to data and actions provided by your application. We’ll show how to use function tools (defined by a JSON schema) and custom tools which work with free form text inputs and outputs.
L8: For Agents API sessions, use Functions to register functions and handle session action requests. The examples in this guide show the Responses API and Chat Completions integrations.
L9: If your application has many functions or large schemas, you can pair function calling with tool search to defer rarely used tools and load them only when the model needs them. Only gpt-5.4 and later models support tool_search.
L10: GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol require the Responses API for tool calling. The Chat Completions examples use GPT-5.6 Terra with reasoning disabled. See the migration guide to update an existing integration.
L11: How it works
L12: Let’s begin by understanding a few key terms about tool calling. After we have a shared vocabulary for tool calling, we’ll show you how it’s done with some practical examples.
L13: Tools - functionality we give the model
L14: A function or tool refers in the abstract to a piece of functionality that we tell the model it has access to. As a model generates a response to a prompt, it may decide that it needs data or functionality provided by a tool to follow the prompt’s instructions.
L15: You could give the model access to tools that:
L16: Get today’s weather for a location
L17: Access account details for a given user ID
L18: Issue refunds for a lost order
L19: Or anything else you’d like the model to be able to know or do as it responds to a prompt.
L20: When we make an API request to the model with a prompt, we can include a list of tools the model could consider using. For example, if we wanted the model to be able to answer questions about the current weather somewhere in the world, we might give it access to a get_weather tool that takes location as an argument.
L21: Tool calls - requests from the model to use tools
L22: A function call or tool call refers to a special kind of response we can get from the model if it examines a prompt, and then determines that in order to follow the instructions in the prompt, it needs to call one of the tools we made available to it.
L23: If the model receives a prompt like “what is the weather in Paris?” in an API request, it could respond to that prompt with a tool call for the get_weather tool, with Paris as the location argument.
L24: Tool call outputs - output we generate for the model
L25: A function call output or tool call output refers to the response a tool generates using the input from a model’s tool call. The tool call output can either be structured JSON or plain text, and it should contain a reference to a specific model tool call (referenced by call_id in the examples to come). To complete our weather example:
L26: The model has access to a get_weather tool that takes location as an argument.
L27: In response to a prompt like “what’s the weather in Paris?” the model returns a tool call that contains a location argument with a value of Paris
L28: The tool call output might return a JSON object (for example, {"temperature": "25", "unit": "C"}, indicating a current temperature of 25 degrees), Image contents, or File contents.
L29: We then send all of the tool definition, the original prompt, the model’s tool call, and the tool call output back to the model to finally receive a text response like:
L30: The weather in Paris today is 25C.
L31: Functions versus tools
L32: A function is a specific kind of tool, defined by a JSON schema. A function definition allows the model to pass data to your application, where your code can access data or take actions suggested by the model.
L33: In addition to function tools, there are custom tools (described in this guide) that work with free text inputs and outputs.
L34: The OpenAI platform also provides built-in tools. These tools enable the model to search the web, run code, access the functionality of an MCP server, and more.
L35: The tool calling flow
L36: Tool calling is a multi-step conversation between your application and a model via the OpenAI API. The tool calling flow has five high level steps:
L37: Make a request to the model with tools it could call
L38: Receive a tool call from the model
L39: Execute code on the application side with input from the tool call
L40: Make a second request to the model with the tool output
L41: Receive a final response from the model (or more tool calls)
L42: With Responses, your application can continue this flow for as many tool calls as the task requires. If you want a framework that packages recurring orchestration around that loop, see how the Responses API compares with the Agents SDK.

L1587: Handling function calls
L1588: When the model calls a function, you must execute it and return the result. Since model responses can include zero, one, or multiple calls, it is best practice to assume there are several.
L1589: The response has an array of tool_calls, each with an id (used later to submit the function result) and a function containing a name and JSON-encoded arguments.

[原文行 2197–2202]
L2197: Formatting results
L2198: The result you pass in the function_call_output message should typically be a string, where the format is up to you (JSON, error codes, plain text, etc.). The model will interpret that string as needed.
L2199: For functions that return images or files, you can pass an array of image or file objects instead of a string.
L2200: If your function has no return value (for example, send_email), return a string that indicates success or failure, such as "success".
L2201: Incorporating results into response
L2202: After appending the results to your messages, you can send them back to the model to get a final response.

L2691: Tool choice
L2692: By default the model will determine when and how many tools to use. You can force specific behavior with the tool_choice parameter.
L2693: Auto: (Default) Call zero, one, or multiple functions. tool_choice: "auto"
L2694: Required: Call one or more functions. tool_choice: "required"
L2695: Forced Function: Call exactly one specific function. tool_choice: {"type": "function", "name": "get_weather"}
L2696: Allowed tools: Restrict the tool calls the model can make to a subset of the tools available to the model.
L2697: When to use allowed_tools
L2698: You might want to configure an allowed_tools list in case you want to make only a subset of tools available across model requests, but not modify the list of tools you pass in, so you can maximize savings from prompt caching.
L2699: 123456789"tool_choice": {
L2700:     "type": "allowed_tools",
L2701:     "mode": "auto",
L2702:     "tools": [
L2703:         { "type": "function", "name": "get_weather" },
L2704:         { "type": "function", "name": "search_docs" }
L2705:     ]
L2706:   }
L2707: }
L2708: You can also set tool_choice to "none" to imitate the behavior of passing no functions.
L2709: When you use tool search, tool_choice still applies to the tools that are currently callable in the turn. This is most useful after you load a subset of tools and want to constrain the model to that subset.
L2710: Parallel function calling
L2711: On supported models beginning with GPT-5, functions can be called in parallel when built-in tools are also available. Built-in tools cannot be included in a parallel function-call batch.
L2712: The model may choose to call multiple functions in a single turn. You can prevent this by setting parallel_tool_calls to false, which ensures exactly zero or one tool is called.
L2713: Note: Currently, if you are using a fine tuned model and the model calls multiple functions in one turn then strict mode will be disabled for those calls.
L2714: Note for gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14: This snapshot of gpt-4.1-nano can sometimes include multiple tool calls for the same tool if parallel tool calls are enabled. It is recommended to disable this feature when using this snapshot.
L2715: Strict mode
L2716: Setting strict to true will ensure function calls reliably adhere to the function schema, instead of being best effort. We recommend always enabling strict mode.
L2717: Under the hood, strict mode works by leveraging our structured outputs feature and therefore introduces a couple requirements:
L2718: additionalProperties must be set to false for each object in the parameters.
L2719: All fields in properties must be marked as required.
L2720: You can denote optional fields by adding null as a type option (see example below).
L2721: If you send strict: true and your schema does not meet the requirements above, the request will be rejected with details about the missing constraints. If you omit strict, the default depends on the API: Responses requests will attempt to normalize your schema into strict mode when possible, and will fall back to non-strict, best-effort function calling if the schema cannot be made compatible with strict mode. When fallback happens, the response tool will show strict: false. Chat Completions requests remain non-strict by default. To opt out of strict mode in Responses and keep non-strict, best-effort function calling, explicitly set strict: false.

L4: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools. Whether you’re building an AI-powered IDE, enhancing a chat interface, or creating custom AI workflows, MCP provides a standardized way to connect LLMs with the context they need. This specification defines the authoritative protocol requirements, based on the TypeScript schema in schema.ts. For implementation guides and examples, visit modelcontextprotocol.io. The key words “MUST”, “MUST NOT”, “REQUIRED”, “SHALL”, “SHALL NOT”, “SHOULD”, “SHOULD NOT”, “RECOMMENDED”, “NOT RECOMMENDED”, “MAY”, and “OPTIONAL” in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
L5: ​
L6: Overview
L7: MCP provides a standardized way for applications to:
L8: Share contextual information with language models
L9: Expose tools and capabilities to AI systems
L10: Build composable integrations and workflows
L11: The protocol uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages to establish communication between:
L12: Hosts: LLM applications that initiate connections
L13: Clients: Connectors within the host application
L14: Servers: Services that provide context and capabilities
L15: MCP takes some inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardizes how to add support for programming languages across a whole ecosystem of development tools. In a similar way, MCP standardizes how to integrate additional context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications.
L16: ​
L17: Key Details
L18: ​
L19: Base Protocol
L20: JSON-RPC message format
L21: Stateless, self-contained requests
L22: Per-request capability negotiation
L23: ​
L24: Features
L25: Servers offer any of the following features to clients:
L26: Resources: Context and data, for the user or the AI model to use
L27: Prompts: Templated messages and workflows for users
L28: Tools: Functions for the AI model to execute
L29: Clients may offer the following features to servers:
L30: Elicitation: Server-initiated requests for additional information from users
L31: ​
L32: Additional Utilities
L33: Configuration
L34: Progress tracking
L35: Cancellation
L36: Error reporting
L37: ​
L38: Extensions
L39: Beyond the core protocol, MCP defines optional extensions that add modular, specialized, or experimental functionality. Extensions are always opt-in and require explicit support from both client and server, negotiated during initialization. Notable extensions include:
L40: Tasks: Asynchronous execution of long-running operations, with polling, mid-flight input, and durable handles
L41: Skills over MCP: Rich, structured instructions for agent workflows, discovered and consumed through MCP
L42: MCP Apps: Interactive UI elements (charts, forms, video players) rendered inline within conversations
L43: ​
L44: Security and Trust & Safety
L45: The Model Context Protocol enables powerful capabilities through arbitrary data access and code execution paths. With this power comes important security and trust considerations that all implementors must carefully address.
L46: ​
L47: Key Principles
L48: User Consent and Control
L49: Users must explicitly consent to and understand all data access and operations
L50: Users must retain control over what data is shared and what actions are taken
L51: Implementors should provide clear UIs for reviewing and authorizing activities
L52: Data Privacy
L53: Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before exposing user data to servers
L54: Hosts must not transmit resource data elsewhere without user consent
L55: User data should be protected with appropriate access controls
L56: Tool Safety
L57: Tools represent arbitrary code execution and must be treated with appropriate caution.
L58: In particular, descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server.
L59: Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool
L60: Users should understand what each tool does before authorizing its use
L61: ​
L62: Implementation Guidelines
L63: While MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level, implementors SHOULD:
L64: Build robust consent and authorization flows into their applications
L65: Provide clear documentation of security implications
L66: Implement appropriate access controls and data protections
L67: Follow security best practices in their integrations
L68: Consider privacy implications in their feature designs

L5: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) allows servers to expose tools that can be invoked by language models. Tools enable models to interact with external systems, such as querying databases, calling APIs, or performing computations. Each tool is uniquely identified by a name and includes metadata describing its schema.
L6: For brevity, the request examples on this page omit the _meta request metadata (io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo, and io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities). Every request MUST include the required _meta fields; see _meta.
L7: ​
L8: User Interaction Model
L9: Tools in MCP are designed to be model-controlled, meaning that the language model can discover and invoke tools automatically based on its contextual understanding and the user’s prompts. However, implementations are free to expose tools through any interface pattern that suits their needs—the protocol itself does not mandate any specific user interaction model.
L10: For trust & safety and security, there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations.Applications SHOULD:
L11: Provide UI that makes clear which tools are being exposed to the AI model
L12: Insert clear visual indicators when tools are invoked
L13: Present confirmation prompts to the user for operations, to ensure a human is in the loop
L14: ​
L15: Capabilities
L16: Servers that support tools MUST declare the tools capability:
L17: {
L18:   "capabilities": {
L19:     "tools": {
L20:       "listChanged": true
L21:     }
L22:   }
L23: }
L24: 
L25: listChanged indicates whether the server will emit notifications when the list of available tools changes. Servers that declare the tools capability MUST respond to tools/list requests with the set of tools currently available to the requesting client. This set MAY be empty and MAY change over time (see List Changed Notification), but MUST NOT vary per-connection or as a side effect of other requests on the connection. The set MAY vary by the authorization presented on the request — for example, returning only the tools the caller’s granted scopes permit — since credentials are per-request input, not connection state. Servers SHOULD return tools in a deterministic order (i.e., the same ordering across requests when the underlying set of tools has not changed). Deterministic ordering enables clients to reliably cache the tool list and improves LLM prompt cache hit rates when tools are included in model context.

L169: Data Types
L170: ​
L171: Tool
L172: A tool definition includes:
L173: name: Unique identifier for the tool
L174: title: Optional human-readable name of the tool for display purposes.
L175: description: Human-readable description of functionality
L176: icons: Optional array of icons for display in user interfaces
L177: inputSchema: JSON Schema defining expected parameters
L178: Follows the JSON Schema usage guidelines
L179: Defaults to 2020-12 if no $schema field is present
L180: MUST be a valid JSON Schema object (not null)
L181: For tools with no parameters, use one of these valid approaches:
L182: { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false } - Recommended: explicitly accepts only empty objects
L183: { "type": "object" } - accepts any object (including with properties)
L184: Properties MAY include an x-mcp-header annotation to expose parameter values as HTTP headers
L185: outputSchema: Optional JSON Schema defining expected output structure
L186: Follows the JSON Schema usage guidelines
L187: Defaults to 2020-12 if no $schema field is present
L188: annotations: Optional properties describing tool behavior
L189: For trust & safety and security, clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.
L190: ​
L191: Tool Names
L192: Tool names SHOULD be between 1 and 128 characters in length (inclusive).
L193: Tool names SHOULD be considered case-sensitive.
L194: The following SHOULD be the only allowed characters: uppercase and lowercase ASCII letters (A-Z, a-z), digits (0-9), underscore (_), hyphen (-), and dot (.)
L195: Tool names SHOULD NOT contain spaces, commas, or other special characters.
L196: Tool names SHOULD be unique within a server.
L197: Example valid tool names:
L198: getUser
L199: DATA_EXPORT_v2
L200: admin.tools.list
L201: Tool name uniqueness is scoped to a single server. Clients or proxies that aggregate tools from multiple servers MAY encounter naming collisions (for example, two servers each exposing a search tool) and SHOULD implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier.The server name (from serverInfo) is not guaranteed to be unique across servers and SHOULD NOT be relied upon for disambiguation.
L202: ​
L203: x-mcp-header
L204: The x-mcp-header extension property allows servers to designate specific tool parameters to be mirrored into HTTP headers when using the Streamable HTTP transport. This enables network intermediaries (load balancers, proxies, WAFs) to route and process requests based on parameter values without parsing the request body. The x-mcp-header property is placed directly within the JSON Schema of the property to be mirrored. Its value specifies the name portion of the resulting Mcp-Param-{name} HTTP header. Constraints on x-mcp-header values:
L205: MUST NOT be empty
L206: MUST match HTTP field-name token syntax (1*tchar, RFC 9110 Section 5.1)
L207: MUST NOT contain control characters, including carriage return (CR, \r) or line feed (LF, \n)
L208: MUST be case-insensitively unique among all x-mcp-header values in the inputSchema
L209: MUST only be applied to parameters with primitive types (integer, string, boolean). Parameters with type number are not permitted. Integer values MUST be within the safe range for integers represented using IEEE754 double-precision floating point numbers (−253+1 to 253−1)
L210: MUST only be applied to properties that are statically reachable from the schema root, as defined in Custom Headers from Tool Parameters, which also defines how header values are extracted from call arguments
L211: Clients using the Streamable HTTP transport MUST reject tool definitions where any x-mcp-header value violates these constraints. Rejection means the client MUST exclude the invalid tool from the result of tools/list. Clients SHOULD log a warning when rejecting a tool definition, including the tool name and the reason for rejection. This ensures that a single malformed tool definition does not prevent other valid tools from being used. Clients using other transports (e.g., stdio) MAY ignore x-mcp-header annotations entirely. Example tool definition with x-mcp-header:
L212: {
L213:   "name": "execute_sql",
L214:   "description": "Execute SQL on Google Cloud Spanner",
L215:   "inputSchema": {
L216:     "type": "object",
L217:     "properties": {
L218:       "region": {
L219:         "type": "string",
L220:         "description": "The region to execute the query in",
L221:         "x-mcp-header": "Region"
L222:       },
L223:       "query": {
L224:         "type": "string",
L225:         "description": "The SQL query to execute"
L226:       }
L227:     },
L228:     "required": ["region", "query"]
L229:   }
L230: }
L231: 
L232: In this example, when the tool is called with "region": "us-west1", the client adds the header Mcp-Param-Region: us-west1 to the HTTP request.
L233: Server developers SHOULD NOT mark sensitive parameters (passwords, API keys, tokens, PII) with x-mcp-header, as header values are visible to network intermediaries.

L266: Resource Links
L267: A tool MAY return links to Resources, to provide additional context or data. In this case, the tool will return a URI that can be subscribed to or fetched by the client:

L295: Embedded resources support the same Resource annotations as regular resources to help clients understand how to use them.

L297: Structured Content
L298: Structured content is returned as a JSON value in the structuredContent field of a result. This can be any JSON value (object, array, string, number, boolean, or null) that conforms to the tool’s outputSchema if one is defined. For backwards compatibility, a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block.
L299: structuredContent is server-produced result data and is unrelated to LLM “structured outputs” (schema-constrained model generation).

L452: Stateful Tools
L453: This section is non-normative guidance for tool design. The protocol has no concept of a state handle; from the wire’s perspective a handle is an ordinary string in a tool result and an ordinary argument to subsequent tool calls.
L454: MCP has no protocol-level session, so a server cannot rely on implicit per-connection state to relate one tool call to the next. Servers that need to maintain state across calls — a shopping cart, an open browser context, a database transaction — should do so by returning an explicit handle from a creation tool and accepting that handle as an argument on subsequent calls. For example, a server that manages a shopping cart might expose:
L455: // → tools/call
L456: { "name": "create_basket", "arguments": {} }
L457: 
L458: // ← result
L459: {
L460:   "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Created basket bsk_a1b2c3" }],
L461:   "structuredContent": { "basket_id": "bsk_a1b2c3" }
L462: }
L463: 
L464: // → tools/call
L465: {
L466:   "name": "add_item",
L467:   "arguments": { "basket_id": "bsk_a1b2c3", "sku": "..." }
L468: }
L469: 
L470: The model is responsible for carrying basket_id forward; the server stores the cart contents under that key and looks them up on each call. When designing handles, servers should consider:
L471: Authorization. For authenticated servers, a handle is a name, not a capability. The server should validate the caller’s authorization against the handle on every call. For unauthenticated servers, where the handle is necessarily a bearer token, it should be generated with sufficient entropy (e.g., a UUIDv4) and given a bounded lifetime.
L472: Opacity. Handles that encode internal structure invite parsing or guessing; opaque identifiers do not.
L473: Lifetime. Because handles outlive any single connection, the server’s retention policy should be stated in the creation tool’s description (e.g., “baskets expire after 24 hours of inactivity”) so the model can see it when deciding to create state.
L474: Expiry errors. A call against an expired or unknown handle should return a tool execution error that says so, so the model can recover by creating a new one.

L476: Error Handling
L477: Tools use two error reporting mechanisms:
L478: Protocol Errors indicate issues with the request structure itself that models are less likely to be able to fix:
L479: Unknown tool
L480: Malformed requests (requests that fail to satisfy CallToolRequest schema)
L481: Server errors
L482: They are returned as standard JSON-RPC errors:
L483: {
L484:   "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L485:   "id": 3,
L486:   "error": {
L487:     "code": -32602,
L488:     "message": "Unknown tool: invalid_tool_name"
L489:   }
L490: }
L491: 
L492: Tool Execution Errors contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters:
L493: API failures
L494: Input validation errors (e.g., date in wrong format, value out of range)
L495: Business logic errors
L496: They are reported in tool results with isError: true:
L497: {
L498:   "jsonrpc": "2.0",
L499:   "id": 4,
L500:   "result": {
L501:     "resultType": "complete",
L502:     "content": [
L503:       {
L504:         "type": "text",
L505:         "text": "Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 08/08/2025."
L506:       }
L507:     ],
L508:     "isError": true
L509:   }
L510: }
L511: 
L512: Clients MAY provide protocol errors to language models, though these are less likely to result in successful recovery. Clients SHOULD provide tool execution errors to language models to enable self-correction.

L514: Security Considerations
L515: Servers MUST:
L516: Validate all tool inputs
L517: Implement proper access controls
L518: Rate limit tool invocations
L519: Sanitize tool outputs
L520: Clients SHOULD:

L660: Step 2: Calling tools
L661: Once the model has access to these tool definitions, it may choose to call them depending on what’s in the model’s context. When the model decides to call an MCP tool, the API will make an request to the remote MCP server to call the tool and put its output into the model’s context. This creates an mcp_call item which looks like this:
L662: 12345678910{
L663:   "id": "mcp_68a6102d8948819c9b1490d36d5ffa4a0679e572a900e618",
L664:   "type": "mcp_call",
L665:   "approval_request_id": null,
L666:   "arguments": "{\"diceRollExpression\":\"2d4 + 1\"}",
L667:   "error": null,
L668:   "name": "roll",
L669:   "output": "4",
L670:   "server_label": "dmcp"
L671: }
L672: This item includes both the arguments the model decided to use for this tool call, and the output that the remote MCP server returned. All models can choose to make multiple MCP tool calls, so you may see several of these items generated in a single API request.
L673: Failed tool calls will populate the error field of this item with MCP protocol errors, MCP tool execution errors, or general connectivity errors. The MCP errors are documented in the MCP spec here.
L674: Approvals
L675: By default, OpenAI will request your approval before any data is shared with a connector or remote MCP server. Approvals help you maintain control and visibility over what data is being sent to an MCP server. We highly recommend that you carefully review (and optionally log) all data being shared with a remote MCP server. A request for an approval to make an MCP tool call creates a mcp_approval_request item in the Response’s output that looks like this:

L679:   "arguments": "{\"diceRollExpression\":\"2d4 + 1\"}",

L4: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) follows a client-host-server architecture where each host can run multiple client instances. MCP is a stateless protocol: every request is self-contained and carries its own protocol version and capabilities. This architecture enables users to integrate AI capabilities across applications while maintaining clear security boundaries and isolating concerns. Built on JSON-RPC, MCP provides a protocol focused on context exchange and sampling coordination between clients and servers.
L5: ​
L6: Core Components
L7: ​
L8: Host
L9: The host process acts as the container and coordinator:
L10: Creates and manages multiple client instances
L11: Controls client connection permissions and lifecycle
L12: Enforces security policies and consent requirements
L13: Handles user authorization decisions
L14: Coordinates AI/LLM integration and sampling
L15: Manages context aggregation across clients
L16: ​
L17: Clients
L18: Each client is created by the host and communicates with exactly one server:
L19: Communicates with exactly one server
L20: Attaches protocol version and capabilities to every request
L21: Routes protocol messages bidirectionally
L22: Manages subscriptions and notifications
L23: Maintains security boundaries between servers
L24: A host application creates and manages multiple clients, with each client having a 1:1 relationship with a particular server.
L25: ​
L26: Servers
L27: Servers provide specialized context and capabilities:
L28: Expose resources, tools and prompts via MCP primitives
L29: Operate independently with focused responsibilities
L30: Request client input (sampling, elicitation, roots) via InputRequiredResult within a reply
L31: Must respect security constraints
L32: Can be local processes or remote services
L33: ​
L34: Design Principles
L35: MCP is built on several key design principles that inform its architecture and implementation:
L36: Servers should be extremely easy to build
L37: Host applications handle complex orchestration responsibilities
L38: Servers focus on specific, well-defined capabilities
L39: Simple interfaces minimize implementation overhead
L40: Clear separation enables maintainable code
L41: Servers should be highly composable
L42: Each server provides focused functionality in isolation
L43: Multiple servers can be combined seamlessly
L44: Shared protocol enables interoperability
L45: Modular design supports extensibility
L46: Servers should not be able to read the whole conversation, nor “see into” other servers
L47: Servers receive only necessary contextual information
L48: Full conversation history stays with the host
L49: Each server maintains isolation
L50: Cross-server interactions are controlled by the host
L51: Host process enforces security boundaries
L52: Features can be added to servers and clients progressively
L53: Core protocol provides minimal required functionality
L54: Additional capabilities can be negotiated as needed
L55: Servers and clients evolve independently
L56: Protocol designed for future extensibility
L57: Backwards compatibility is maintained
L58: ​
L59: Capability Negotiation
L60: The Model Context Protocol uses a capability-based negotiation system where clients and servers declare their supported features on each request. Clients include their capabilities in _meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities on every request. Servers advertise their capabilities in response to server/discover, which clients may call before any other request for up-front capability discovery.
L61: Servers declare capabilities like tool support, resource subscriptions, and prompt templates
L62: Clients declare capabilities like sampling support and elicitation handling
L63: Both parties must respect declared capabilities throughout the interaction
L64: Additional capabilities can be negotiated through extensions to the protocol
L65: Each capability unlocks specific protocol features on a per-request basis. For example:
L66: Implemented server features must be advertised in the server’s capabilities
L67: Receiving resource update notifications requires opening a subscriptions/listen stream with the desired resource URIs
L68: Tool invocation requires the server to declare tool capabilities
L69: This capability negotiation ensures clients and servers have a clear understanding of supported functionality while maintaining protocol extensibility.

L511: ### Non-prompt injection related risks
L512: 
L513: Custom MCPs introduce other risks unrelated to prompt injection attacks:
L514: 
L515: - **Write actions can increase both the usefulness and the risks of MCP servers**, because they make it possible for the server to take potentially destructive actions rather than only providing information back to ChatGPT. ChatGPT currently requires manual confirmation in any conversation before write actions can be taken. The confirmation will flag potentially sensitive data but you should only use write actions in situations where you have carefully considered, and are comfortable with, the possibility that ChatGPT might make a mistake involving such an action. It is possible for write actions to occur even if the MCP server has tagged the action as read only, making it even more important that you trust the custom MCP server before deploying to ChatGPT.
L516: - **Any MCP server may receive sensitive data as part of querying**. Even when the server is not malicious, it will have access to whatever data ChatGPT supplies during the interaction, potentially including sensitive data the user may earlier have provided to ChatGPT. For instance, such data could be included in queries ChatGPT sends to the MCP server when using deep research or chat app tools.
L517: 
L518: ### Connecting to trusted servers
L519: 
L520: We recommend that you do not connect to a custom MCP server unless you know and trust the underlying application.
L521: 
L522: For example, choose official servers hosted by the service providers themselves. Connect to the Stripe server hosted by Stripe at `mcp.stripe.com` instead of an unofficial Stripe MCP server hosted by a third party. Because few official MCP servers are available today, you may consider a server hosted by an organization that proxies requests to another service through an API. Only connect after you have reviewed how the organization uses your data and verified that you can trust the server. When building and connecting to your own MCP server, double-check that it's the correct server. Be careful about the data you provide in response to requests and how you treat data sent to you when OpenAI calls your MCP server.
L523: 
L524: Your remote MCP server permits others to connect OpenAI to your services and allows OpenAI to access, send and receive data, and take action in these services. Avoid putting any sensitive information in the JSON for your tools, and avoid storing any sensitive information from ChatGPT users accessing your remote MCP server.
L525: 
L526: As someone building an MCP server, don't put anything malicious in your tool definitions.
